title: Your Story Bank
oneLiner: Write eight to ten of your own stories in STAR form and check they cover every competency interviewers probe.
keyTakeaway: You can't invent a good story under pressure, but you can prepare eight to ten in advance that between them cover every common question. Most questions are variations on about a dozen themes, so the work is choosing and rehearsing the stories, not memorising answers to hundreds of questions.
explanation:
Strong candidates walk in with a prepared set of stories and adapt them to whatever is asked. A single good story, such as a difficult project you led, can answer "your biggest impact", "a conflict with a colleague" and "a decision with incomplete data", depending on which part you emphasise.

Write each story in STAR form below and tag the competencies it shows. The coverage grid tells you which themes you have no story for yet. Aim for at least one per theme and two for the ones that come up in almost every loop: conflict, failure, and impact. In a full day of interviews you may be asked about conflict three times by three different people, and you should be able to give each a different story.

Good source material: projects from your last two or three years (older ones sound stale), incidents, launches that slipped, disagreements about design or priorities, people you helped, and things you changed that nobody asked you to. Write the Action part in detail even though you'll only say a fraction of it; the detail is what you'll need for follow-up questions.

Your stories are saved in this browser only (the dashboard's progress export includes them). Use "Copy all as text" to keep a copy somewhere safer. The Behavioral Mock Round uses these stories, so you can practise choosing the right one for each question.
